records.text: 83. Samoa faces significant environmental challenges, exacerbated by its status as a small island developing State. Despite its minimal contribution to global pollution, Samoa is disproportionately affected by climate change, plastic pollution and hazardous waste, endangering its environment, which is central to the Samoan way of life. 84. Samoa, like many small island developing States, is often on the receiving end of decisions and action taken by other States and businesses, with limited leverage. The arrival of low-quality plastic products leads to an ecological catastrophe in a place where plastic pollution cannot be processed and contained. While some actions can be taken at the national level, the importance of multilateralism and international environmental agreements cannot be overstated for the protection of the people and the environment of Samoa and other small island developing States. In this context, a strong plastic pollution treaty in line with human rights, including the right to information, the right to a clean, healthy and sustainable environment and the right to science are key to properly frame effective and legitimate solutions and remedies. 85. Samoa has championed the environment and human rights in international forums. It has ratified the major multilateral environmental agreements on chemicals and wastes, taken a strong stance on several global environmental issues and demonstrated high ambition in the negotiations on an international treaty on plastic pollution. 86. Nationally, the efforts to manage wastes and pollution are commendable, particularly through the legislative framework and international cooperation. However, the Constitution and legal framework have yet to explicitly recognize the right to a clean, healthy and sustainable environment. 87. The waste management infrastructure in Samoa, while relatively advanced for the region, struggles with capacity and enforcement issues. The Tafaigata and Vaia’ata landfill sites are nearing capacity, and there is a pressing need for effective waste recovery and recycling programmes. While the introduction of a waste levy on items like PET bottles and aluminium cans is a positive step, broader implementation and enforcement are necessary. 88. E-waste and hazardous substances like asbestos and pesticides pose additional risks. The lack of adequate data and monitoring hampers effective management and enforcement. Initiatives like the extended producer responsibility schemes for e-waste and the proposed ban on highly hazardous pesticides like paraquat are crucial steps forward. 89. Samoan traditional practices and community-based governance systems offer valuable lessons in sustainable living and environmental stewardship. Strengthening those systems, along with enhancing legal frameworks and international cooperation, will be vital for Samoa to protect its environment and ensure the health and well-being of its people.

On 5 October 2024, about three weeks prior to the Special Rapporteur’s arrival in Samoa, a New Zealand naval ship, HMNZS Manawanui, ran aground about 2 km off the south coast of Upolu. Manawanui was a research vessel and was carrying out survey work of a reef. Reports suggest that, at the time of sinking, the ship was carrying 950 tons of diesel fuel. Moreover, it is well known that research laboratories employ hazardous substances and generate hazardous waste. 81. In the days following the sinking of the ship, local residents reported seeing and smelling oil and fish covered in oil, and a leak from the engine room was confirmed. As a result, a 20 km stretch of coastal area was closed to fishing, affecting the livelihoods and food source of local communities. On 15 October, salvage work began, with the New Zealand Defence Force assisted by the Government of Samoa, Maritime New Zealand and the Samoan Marine Pollution and Advisory Committee. Moreover, a naval court of inquiry investigated the loss of the ship and by the end of November, it found that the ship had sunk due to human error. Concerns were raised about the pace of salvage work and the need for an international independent inquiry to ensure impartiality and accountability. Furthermore, affected communities expressed frustration at insufficient information-sharing. 82. The Special Rapporteur engaged with the Samoan and New Zealand authorities during the visit and stressed the need for full and transparent disclosure of the inventory of the hazardous substances in the vessel, the type and volume of fuel and other crucial information necessary for effective mitigation and restoration measures. He also reiterates that communities and fisherfolk should have access to effective remedies, including adequate compensation and environmental rehabilitation. While the naval ship may benefit from certain immunities of jurisdiction, accountability and adequate reparations must be guaranteed.

records.text: 77. Given its geographical location and condition, the national life and economic activities of Samoa are largely dependent on maritime transportation. While in Apia, the Special Rapporteur engaged with the Samoa Ports Authority, which oversees the operation and management of the country’s seaports, and visited the Matautu Port, which handles 97 per cent of all foreign trade cargo for the country. 78. The International Convention for the Prevention of Pollution From Ships, 1973, obliges States to provide waste reception facilities to enable the sound management of wastes produced by vessels. In Samoa, the Marine Pollution Prevention Act 2008 provides for marine pollution prevention, including by providing for and regulating waste reception facilities and responses to marine pollution incidents from vessels. However, it seems that the Act does not fully reflect the revised annex V of the International Convention, which entered into force in 2013, including the prohibition of many overboard discharges. Furthermore, the Special Rapporteur learned of plans to increase the number of cruise ships coming to Samoa. Adequate port reception facilities for the sound management of waste are therefore critical to process garbage, oily wastes, sewage and cargo residue, among other discharges. Samoa currently has limited or no capacity to receive some of those waste streams, as there is also no suitable means for ultimate disposal. 79. There are existing national plans to deal with some of those waste streams. For example, for used oils, a national used oil management plan is under development. There are also efforts by the Secretariat of the Pacific Regional Environment Programme, the Ministry of Natural Resources and Environment and the Samoa Recycling and Waste Management Association to work towards a management and disposal solution, including re-export or take-back schemes for used oils. The Special Rapporteur notes that plans for the management of waste from ships could be integrated into broader national plans for waste management, in order to capture greater synergy and efficiency.

records.text: 70. At the national level, the agriculture sector constitutes two fifths of the gross domestic product of Samoa and employs nearly two thirds of the Samoan workforce. At the household level, over 97 per cent of all households in Samoa are engaged in agriculture. Some 19 per cent of them rely on agriculture as their main source of income. 71. Samoa uses an average of 6.33 kg of pesticides per hectare, ranking forty-ninth in the world in terms of pesticide use per area of cropland, based on 2022 data from the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO). The Pesticides Regulations 2011 provide for the registration, control and management of pesticides in Samoa. They also establish a Pesticides Technical Committee and empower the Minister of Agriculture and Fisheries to appoint a Registrar for the purposes of enforcement. Under the Regulations, a person cannot import, manufacture, pack, repack, label, store, sell, distribute, advertise, apply, possess or use any pesticide unless it has been registered and the person has obtained a pesticide dealer’s licence. They also provide for a special permit for restricted pesticides. The Regulations establish rules for the storage, packing, labelling, advertisement, handling and disposal of pesticides. 72. Nonetheless, in practice, the improper use and disposal of pesticides in Samoa is rampant. During his visit, the Special Rapporteur was told that pesticides are often decanted into unlabelled containers and are sometimes distributed to users without a licence. Pesticide containers are also sometimes used to store water and feed animals. Precautionary measures such as maintaining a buffer zone to prevent drifting or run-off are seldom followed. Furthermore, pesticide containers are disposed of together with general waste and there is no specific sorting requirement or mechanism. 73. There are several barriers to the proper enforcement of the Pesticides Regulations. One major issue is the availability of data and the traceability of pesticides. While there may be some data on pesticide imports, there is almost no data on pesticide use, exposure of workers and communities, and impacts on soil and water, among other key information. Furthermore, the cross-cutting resourcing issue affects monitoring and enforcement of pesticides. People also have little awareness of the impacts of pesticides on health and the environment, and they are not provided with training or guidance on how to handle the pesticides they are using. 74. The use of highly toxic or persistent pesticides, including those banned in their countries of origin or where they are produced, is a critical problem. The use of paraquat, for example, is an ongoing debate in Samoa. Reportedly, concerns about the toxic effects of paraquat in Samoa were first raised in 1977 when the country’s medical authorities proposed a total ban due to rising rates of self-poisoning. As little as one teaspoon of paraquat can cause death. In the 1980s, two thirds of all deaths by suicide in Samoa were attributed to pesticide poisoning. Most of those deaths were found to be impulsive acts of self-harm among young people with low suicidal intent. Given the easy access to it, paraquat is still commonly used in suicide and even in a recent murder. Between 2004 and 2018, 74 deaths were caused by paraquat – the youngest victim being a 12-year-old girl in 2015. With respect to long‐term exposure, several studies found that frequent use of paraquat can increase the risk of Parkinson’s disease and several types of cancer, among other adverse health impacts. Consequently, more than 70 countries have banned paraquat. The Special Rapporteur saw workers applying paraquat in Samoa without adequate personal protective equipment and while wearing shorts and flip-flops. 75. Civil society organizations working on health and environmental policies in Samoa have been calling for a ban in the country. In 2023, the Ministry of Natural Resources and Environment and FAO conducted a pesticide management gap analysis, the official findings of which are yet to be released. In response to questions on the delay in releasing the findings, the Government asserted that a ban must consider scientific analysis, best alternative solutions, social and economic considerations, and legal and procedural requirements. It also argued that there is insufficient conclusive evidence of paraquat’s significant toxicity and that there are no viable alternatives. The Special Rapporteur notes that this claim is at odds with the scientific studies and the bans in many other countries. Fiji, for example, banned paraquat in 2020 and uses alternatives that are less harmful to human health and the environment. 76. Farmers shared with the Special Rapporteur their concerns about not using common and highly toxic pesticides, fearing that alternatives may be risky, expensive or unproven. The Special Rapporteur explained the distinction between highly hazardous pesticides, like paraquat and glyphosate, and less hazardous alternatives, noting that the former need to be replaced by the latter. Moreover, the traditional farming system of Samoa relied solely on organic practices such as natural regeneration of soils, manual weeding and traditional natural remedies for pests. During a visit to a community, the Special Rapporteur asked how the community dealt with weeds prior to the introduction of pesticides. He was told they used knives and mechanical tools, which was more labour intensive. People therefore turned to those pesticides for convenience. While the Special Rapporteur recognizes that pesticides can appear to be convenient, he reiterates the importance of choosing less or non-harmful options and encourages a move towards the application of integrated pest management. Behavioural changes are necessary.

records.text: 66. The number of cars in Samoa is steadily increasing, contributing to another waste stream the country cannot process. During his visit, the Special Rapporteur saw many abandoned cars lying around in different sites, with their chemicals slowly contaminating the environment around them. Tyres produced from rubber and petroleum-based compounds are a problematic car component. The production, use and disposal of tyres releases numerous heavy metals, plastics, polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons and other compounds that can be persistent and toxic independently or as chemical cocktails. Tyres can also retain water, making them ideal breeding grounds for disease-carrying mosquitos and bacteria. 67. An estimated 6,700 tons of tyres reach end of life annually across Pacific island countries. The Special Rapporteur was informed that the import of used tyres is a common practice in Samoa, enabled by limited control over the quality of tyre imports. While used tyres may be cheaper, their lifetime is much shorter, accelerating the generation of waste tyres in the country. In Samoa, end-of-life tyres are usually landfilled or illegally burned or stockpiled. When burned in the open, tyres can release potent hazardous particulates such as carbon monoxide, sulfur oxides, nitrogen oxides, dioxins, furans, polychlorinated biphenyls and metals like mercury, arsenic and nickel, among others. 68. The recycling of end-of-life tyres presents major challenges owing to their complex structure and composition. Furthermore, there are concerns about the health risks associated with the recycling of rubber. For example, the use of crumb rubber in the construction of artificial turf on playgrounds and football fields has been linked to lymphoma and leukaemia. Such applications could also have adverse impacts on the environment from weathering and water run-off leaching into the ground. The Special Rapporteur was also informed of plans to create waste-to-energy plants based on the burning of different materials, including tyres. He expresses serious doubts about the soundness of that approach in view of the release of toxic chemicals into the air, even when filters are used. 69. In addition to abandoned vehicles and waste tyres, electric cars are being brought into Samoa. Samoa has taken important steps towards climate change mitigation. One of the country’s major goals under the National Strategic Plan is to achieve 70 per cent renewable energy use by the end of 2031. As of 2022, renewable energy sources accounted for about 45 per cent of the total installed capacity in Samoa. While electric vehicles will contribute to the reduction of greenhouse gas emissions, they also create new waste streams. The lithium batteries in electric vehicles are highly toxic and present risks of explosion if mishandled. Therefore, they are classified as hazardous waste and require certain measures and specifications for their safe transportation and disposal. The Special Rapporteur was told of future plans to ship the waste batteries out of Samoa. Yet, it seems that there is currently no clear management plan beyond interim storage in fortified containers. Any plan involving the shipping of waste batteries out of Samoa must also consider the permits and procedures required for Samoa to fulfil its obligations under the Basel and Waigani Conventions.

records.text: 62. Information about the extent of asbestos exposure and contamination in the Pacific region was very limited until a regional baseline survey was conducted in 2014 through the PacWaste programme. The survey identified over 187,000 m2 of non-residential asbestos in 11 Pacific island countries, 78 per cent of which was classified as high or moderate risk. Moreover, the survey revealed that new materials containing asbestos were being imported in the region. The results of the survey highlighted the need for regional action. 63. In 2017, together with other Pacific islands, Samoa endorsed an initiative to ban or restrict the importation, reuse and resale of products and waste containing asbestos. In 2021, PacWaste Plus developed an Asbestos Management Legislative Reform Pathway which outlines the steps necessary to institute bans on asbestos. While a ban on asbestos has not yet been instituted in the legislative framework of Samoa, there are laws governing the management of asbestos. In June 2014, the Occupational Safety and Health Regulations 2014 were introduced. Part 11, section 65, specifically covers work with asbestos. The regulations state that a licence must be obtained to remove asbestos cement greater than 10 m2 in area or greater than 0.5 m2 in insulation. The Waste Management Act 2010 and the Lands Surveys and Environment Act 1989 are also relevant to the management of asbestos, although they do not specifically address asbestos. 64. Based on a survey of 2,800 properties in Samoa, asbestos fibres, chrysotile, amosite and crocidolite were detected in 18 of the 48 samples analysed. Some of the locations that have materials containing asbestos include the Meteorological Station on Upolu and a timber treatment facility in Savai’i. However, only one residential building was suspected of having such material. Twelve of the sites assessed present a moderate to high risk and some of them are unsecured, with evidence of people being on the site. The Special Rapporteur warns that this is particularly problematic considering the increase in the incidence and severity of cyclones, due to climate change. Such extreme weather events have the effect of disturbing housing and construction, which in turn exposes the population to the inhalation of deadly asbestos fibres. 65. The Special Rapporteur was informed about designated areas for the disposal of asbestos during his visit to Tafaigata. Nonetheless, he stresses the need for improved handling and disposal procedures, such as ensuring immediate cover after placement in cells. Safe management can only be ensured with adequate monitoring.

records.text: 56. Electronic waste (e-waste) is one of the fastest growing solid waste streams in the world. Every year, millions of mobile phones, computers, televisions, refrigerators and other electrical goods are discarded as they break down or become obsolete. E-waste is regarded as hazardous waste as it contains a variety of hazardous substances such as cadmium, lead, chromium, mercury, dioxins or polychlorinated biphenyls. At least four of these chemicals are included in the World Health Organization’s list of “10 chemicals of public health concern”. E-waste exposure may be linked to adverse neurodevelopment impacts, including behavioural and learning abilities, increased rates of stillbirths or premature birth and reduced lung function, among others. Children and women are at high risk due to their unique vulnerabilities. Toxic substances released from e-waste could cross the placenta and contaminate breastmilk. Moreover, fetuses, babies and young children have rapidly developing systems, and exposure at those critical stages could cause irreparable harm, affecting them for the rest of their lives. 57. Government entities, businesses and households in Samoa are becoming increasingly reliant on electronic goods to perform their daily functions due to technology development, better access to electricity and the availability of more affordable consumer electronics. Information available on e-waste generation, imports and exports in Samoa is very limited. The Ministry of Customs and Revenues collects some data on imports and exports of electronic goods. However, existing customs Harmonized System coding has no special codes to distinguish between used goods or e-waste and general electronic and electrical goods. The lack of a mechanism to track the transboundary movement of e-waste to and from Samoa undermines its capacity to fulfil its obligations under the Basel and Waigani Conventions. 58. Household e-waste is usually disposed of together with other general waste in Samoa. The Government organizes free collection of bulky waste, including household e-waste, three to four times a year. Most of the collected waste is then transported to the landfill sites without appropriate storage facilities. During his visit to the Tafaigata landfill, the Special Rapporteur saw mountains of e-waste out in the open, directly exposed to rainfall, risking contamination of the surrounding environment. 59. The Ministry of Finance collects some data on write-off electrical equipment from government ministries. All write-off electrical equipment is collected and stored at a government storage area. However, it has been suggested that storage conditions are inadequate. The write-off electrical equipment is eventually sold in public auctions where refurbishing operators or households buy the equipment at a lower cost. Nevertheless, the remaining equipment is disposed of at the landfill. 60. Many end-of-life electronics contain valuable and recoverable material such as copper, steel and gold. However, the inappropriate recovery of these materials can have detrimental impacts on health. There are several, mostly small-scale, refurbishing operations of electrical equipment in Samoa. The reused recovered parts from old electronic equipment are mostly limited to the separable parts which do not require special dismantling operations. Meanwhile, while there is a licensing process for waste pickers at the landfill site. The recovery of valuable materials from e-waste by waste pickers using unsafe practices like burning is a concern, particularly given the lack of adequate monitoring. 61. The European Union PacWaste Plus programme aims to provide technical support and training on safe handling and dismantling of e-waste. The Special Rapporteur was pleased to learn of extended producer responsibility schemes for e-waste in Samoa. In 2024, the Ministry of Natural Resources and Environment signed a memorandum of understanding with Blue Orca New Zealand for the implementation of a take-back programme considering the lack of recycling options in Samoa. Under the scheme, all types and brands of e-waste are covered. The Samoa and Tokelau Association of Recyclers provides support with the collection and compilation of the e-waste, which is then shipped under the Moana Taka Partnership for recycling abroad. By February 2025, Samsung, Blue Orca and S.T.A.R had collected and shipped 12,911 kg of e-waste from Samoa to New Zealand under the Moana Taka Partnership.

records.text: 48. About 12.2 million tons of plastic waste are estimated to enter the ocean annually. Samoan traditional and cultural value systems include a deep reverence for the ocean and the environment; at their core is the belief that humans and the natural world are interconnected. Studies of samples taken in the ocean region between New Zealand, Samoa, Tahiti and Rapa Nui found microplastics in 97 per cent of the fish species examined in comparison to the global average of 67 per cent, showing the disproportionate impacts on small island developing States. Samoans are prone to feeling the negative impacts of marine plastic pollution more acutely given the strong cultural connection and reliance on the ocean for food, tourism and other forms of economic gain. 49. Much of the marine plastic pollution in Samoa originates from sources thousands of kilometres away. Plastic imports in Samoa almost doubled between 2020 and 2023, according to data collected from the Samoa Bureau for Statistics and analysed by the Samoa Conservation Society. A 2019 study estimated the annual consumption of plastic products at 6,830 tons, equivalent to about 34.5 kg per person. The tourism sector is a key contributor to plastic waste, generating about 20 per cent of all plastic waste in the country, and airline tourism constitutes 75 per cent of this waste. A 2020 national quantification of plastic waste found that, on average, tourists generate almost 40 times more plastic waste than Samoan residents. 50. Plastics and many of the chemicals they contain persist in the environment, with the natural decomposition of plastics estimated to take hundreds to thousands of years. Plastic materials also break down into smaller fragments as microplastics or nanoplastics. These particles are difficult to detect, hard to remove and are easily ingested by animals, ultimately also making their way into the human body. 51. The negative impacts of plastics must be considered at all stages of their life cycle and across the value chain. Plastics originate as fossil fuels and have a large greenhouse gas footprint. The extraction of fossil fuels and the transport, decomposition and possible incineration of plastics emits significant amounts of greenhouse gases and other pollutants. Therefore, plastics directly contribute to exacerbating the climate emergency to which Samoa is vulnerable. The Special Rapporteur commends Samoa on its push for a full life-cycle approach in the plastics treaty negotiations. Global environmental injustice needs to be tackled, including by protecting small islands against the influx of plastic pollution. There is a need for legally binding obligations to control and phase out the most harmful plastic products and chemicals of concern, including by ensuring transparency and traceability of plastic chemicals to protect human health and the environment throughout the full life cycle of plastics. 52. As in most other small island developing States, the reliance of Samoa on imported products limits its ability to influence product design, making it dependent on specifications and standards established in plastic producing States. The production of plastics is associated with 13,000 to 16,000 chemicals, some of which are highly toxic. These chemicals can be released during extraction or manufacturing, when plastic is used, or even when plastic becomes waste, leaching into the soil or water sources. There is a constant stream of plastic products entering Samoa. However, information on the full chemical composition of these products is rarely disclosed. In a small market like Samoa, some external companies have de facto oligopoly, leading to limited or no competition among producers. This situation limits the ability of consumers to influence or put pressure on the dominant companies and ask them to respect transparency or environmental standards. Moreover, market regulation and the imposition of import restrictions could be very resource intensive for small island developing States like Samoa. These dynamics perpetuate cross-border environmental injustice and inequality in access to information. 53. In an attempt to regulate the flow of plastics entering the country, in 2018, Samoa introduced a plastic ban, which was to be implemented in stages. Since 2019, the regulation has prohibited the import, manufacturing, sale and export of plastic shopping bags, plastic packaging bags and plastic straws, and in 2020 the ban extended to Styrofoam containers and cups. The National Waste Management Strategy 2019–2023 also promotes the three Rs (reduce, reuse and recycle) approach. The strategy and ban are consistent with the waste hierarchy principles which prioritize prevention of waste generation over waste management and disposal. However, reports suggest that plastic bags and plastic straws are still in community circulation, pointing at the cross-cutting enforcement challenge. 54. During his visit, the Special Rapporteur was alarmed to learn of good practices that had been reversed, hampering prevention efforts. For decades, Coca-Cola Amatil Limited bottled soft drinks locally in Samoa in reusable glass bottles. Consumers were encouraged to return the empty glass bottles, upon which there was a deposit. Most bottles were reused multiple times under that system, limiting littering and waste. In 2021, the reusable glass bottles were replaced by the company with plastic bottles produced in other countries. That business decision to switch packaging materials led to an immediate increase in plastic pollution on the island and in the surrounding marine environment. Reportedly, only a few months after the decision, Coca-Cola contributed to one third of the plastic bottle waste in Samoa. After his visit, the Special Rapporteur sent a letter to the company. 55. The Special Rapporteur is concerned that plastic producers are placing the plastic burden on and externalizing the costs of plastic pollution to developing States that lack the capacity and resources to confront the global plastic tide. The negotiations on a legally binding treaty on plastic pollution present an opportunity to secure transparency and accountability of plastic producers and the States in which they are domiciled. The Special Rapporteur stresses the importance of enabling access to information under the treaty, especially on volumes of plastics produced and chemicals of concern in plastic products. Such information is critical for informed decision-making and for effective monitoring and enforcement, including with respect to establishing reductions in plastic production. In line with calls by Samoa, the instrument should also include a financial mechanism supported by contributions from plastic producers to help developing States implement plastic waste management measures, including through access to resources, technology transfer and capacity-building. The Special Rapporteur notes that explicit references to human rights in the treaty, including the right to access information, the right to a clean, healthy and sustainable environment and the right to development, are critical to the proper framing of effective and legitimate solutions.

records.text: 43. Samoa has consistently engaged regional and international partners to reinforce national waste management and recycling capacity. The Special Rapporteur met with some of the country’s development partners during his visit. The Secretariat of the Pacific Regional Environment Programme is a key player in this field and manages several waste management programmes and projects at the regional level. It ensures that factors important for Pacific small island developing States are considered and that a regional perspective is taken when designing and implementing projects. 44. One of the most prominent waste management projects in the region is the Japanese Technical Cooperation Project for Promotion of Regional Initiative on Solid Management in Pacific Island Countries, which was implemented through a partnership between Pacific small island developing States, the Government of Japan and the Secretariat of the Pacific Regional Environment Programme. Between 2000 and 2005, the Japan International Cooperation Agency and the Secretariat worked together on bilateral technical cooperation projects. For example, Tafaigata landfill site was upgraded using the Fukuoka method as a showcase facility for other Pacific small island developing States and donors. 45. The PacWaste Plus programme is another regional waste management programme funded by the European Union and implemented by the Secretariat of the Pacific Regional Environment Programme. It aims to contribute to improved data collection, development of policy and regulatory frameworks, enhanced private sector engagement and enhanced human capacity. In 2020, the initiative assessed the state of the legislative framework governing waste management and in 2023, published a National Waste Audit Report. The programme identified e-waste management as a priority for Samoa. 46. Two of the recycling organizations the Special Rapporteur met with are beneficiaries of the Moana Taka Partnership, which is supported by the PacWaste Plus. That Partnership seeks to address one of the major hurdles to recycling in Samoa: shipping of recyclable waste. The China Navigation Company/Swire Shipping have partnered with the Secretariat of the Pacific Regional Environment Programme to utilize empty shipping containers to transport recyclable waste generated by residential or non-business sources to other Swire-serviced ports in countries with recycling or disposal facilities. Under the scheme, container hire and transport are covered by the Moana Taka Partnership. However, the shipper would still need to cover and handle loading and unloading logistics, authorization fees to comply with the requirements of the relevant multilateral environmental agreements, customs and permit fees, insurance and other expenses. While the Secretariat can assist local recycling organizations with identifying requirements, navigating those procedures can be challenging for organizations with limited capacity and funding. The Special Rapporteur notes that the Secretariat’s capacity is also limited, as its team covers the whole region. 47. Those efforts are good examples of synergizing waste management initiatives, leveraging public-private partnerships and encouraging community engagement for the environmentally sound management of waste. One common complaint the Special Rapporteur received was that pilot projects were being initiated but not sustained over the long-term.

records.text: 41. Considering the challenges to landfilling, recovery and recycling emerge as an attractive solution to divert waste away from landfills. Yet, recycling mainly targets high value and recyclable waste streams. For recycling activities to be economically viable, it is critical to achieve economies of scale. This is difficult in a small island State like Samoa. Therefore, currently, the main method local recycling organizations resort to is the stockpiling of recyclable waste to be exported for recycling abroad. Yet, additional barriers exist including challenges around collection and servicing remote and dispersed communities, high freight costs due to long distances and complicated procedures to comply with regional and international regulations on waste export, among others. These challenges render most recycling solutions uneconomical. 42. After two years of consultation with the private sector and other stakeholders, Samoa is planning to introduce a waste levy on several items, including polyethylene terephthalate (PET) plastic bottles and aluminium cans. The Special Rapporteur was encouraged to hear about discussions on expanding that scheme to other items.

records.text: 38. There are two approved landfill sites in Samoa: Tafaigata on Upolu and Vaia’ata on Savai’i. In 2003, Tafaigata was upgraded from an open dumpsite to a semi-aerobic waste landfill with technical assistance and support from the Japan International Cooperation Agency. In 2006, Vaia’ata was constructed following the same model. The World Bank Group partnered with the Japan International Cooperation Agency to install healthcare waste incinerators, and the European Union funded the construction of special lagoons for the disposal of sewage and sludge at both landfill sites. 39. The Vaia’ata landfill site is almost a third of the size of the Tafaigata site and has fewer facilities. Tafaigata has designated areas for asbestos burial and disaster waste storage, as well as designated areas for recycling activities, while Vaia’ata lacks such capacity. Nevertheless, according to the Samoa state of the environment report 2023, Tafaigata is expected to reach capacity by 2032 if waste recovery is not effectively carried out. Currently, the engineered waste cells at Tafaigata are reportedly full and waste is being stored in areas with no lining. In the absence of lining, toxic and contaminated leachate can seep into the soil and pollute underground water, posing serious risks to the environment and neighbouring communities. In addition, the good functioning of the Fukuoka method requires constant maintenance, which currently seems to be lacking. 40. The Ministry of Natural Resources and Environment outsources the daily operation and management of the landfill sites to private companies. However, monitoring of those operations seems problematic. Records of the volumes and types of waste collected are not kept and environmental quality testing is not conducted on a regular basis, making it difficult to assess the environmental impact of waste disposal. When he visited the landfill site, the Special Rapporteur spoke with workers who were unaware of the types and impacts of chemicals released from the on-site incinerator. Moreover, some workers were not wearing adequate personal protective equipment, with one worker suggesting that the hot weather made wearing closed shoes uncomfortable. The regulatory and monitoring shortcomings are primarily related to financial and human resources at the Ministry of Natural Resources and Environment, which is overstretched.

records.text: 35. The Ministry of Natural Resources and Environment extends waste collection services to all Samoan households free of charge. Meanwhile, the commercial sector is responsible for its own waste disposal either by transporting the waste directly to the landfill or by paying a private contractor for that service. The Ministry of Natural Resources and Environment outsources waste collection to private contractors, with each contractor covering a defined collection zone. There are specific collection points within each zone where trucks stop to collect waste. Households typically leave their waste on a raised platform for collection, away from scavenging animals. For households without a collection point, waste is collected only if an individual is waiting for the arrival of the truck. On average, waste collection is offered twice a week. A 2017 study on the state of waste collection on Upolu and Savai’i found that out of 6,260 collection points on Upolu, 84 per cent contained waste and 15 per cent were empty. It also found that about 60 per cent of the waste on the designated road was collected, while the remaining 40 per cent was not collected. 36. Most of the organic waste in Samoa, such as food scraps or grass trimmings, is sustainably managed within communities. Regular awareness-raising campaigns encourage the use of green waste as mulch for gardens or for feeding animals. Waste collection contractors are also instructed not to collect organic waste from communities, except in the main town area. The small percentage of organic waste that reaches the landfill site is mostly attributed to self-haulers or businesses, and the Ministry of Natural Resources and Environment has provided space within the landfill for composting operations. Composting has long been practised traditionally in Samoa. This is testament to the fact that Samoans have lived for thousands of years relying on their knowledge and closeness to nature in a way that kept them thriving and their environment healthy. Samoan traditional practices and knowledge should be promoted and integrated in all waste management efforts. 37. The Samoa state of the environment report 2013 asserted that only 11 per cent of waste generated reached the two landfill sites. The Samoa state of the environment report 2023 indicated that 80 per cent of the waste generated on Upolu reached the Tafaigata landfill. Given that waste management practices in Samoa are primarily limited to landfilling, it is likely that much of the waste is littered, buried or incinerated. In this regard, awareness-raising and close coordination between national and village authorities are critical to bring about the necessary behavioural changes and to strengthen enforcement.

records.text: 33. Samoa is inundated with increasingly diverse waste streams. Plastics, e-waste, end‐of‐life vehicles, tyres, pesticide containers and other hazardous materials pose pervasive environmental threats, jeopardizing the health of the Samoan people, land and marine environment. Data on the amounts and types of waste generated in Samoa is limited, and regular waste assessment is not conducted. A report by the United Nations Development Programme found discrepancies in estimates of waste generation in Samoa: where a World Bank audit estimated waste generation at 0.28 kg per person per day, the National Waste Management Strategy indicated 1.06 kg per person per day, and a report by the Asian Development Bank suggested between 0.38 to 0.46 kg per person per day, with amounts in urban centres like Apia likely to be significantly higher than in villages and rural areas. 34. Over the past decade, Samoa has made significant efforts to deal with solid waste management. The authorities collaborated with local, regional and international partners to gradually improve solid waste collection, increase the capacity of landfill sites and develop the necessary waste management regulatory and policy instruments, such as the Waste Management Act 2010 and the National Waste Management Strategy 2019–2023. The Ministry of Natural Resources and Environment is the largest government agency in the country, with 16 divisions. For about 20 years, the Division of Environment and Conservation has overseen the waste management sector with about 30 staff members working under very limited capacity. In 2023, a new Waste Management and Pollution Control Division was established, demonstrating the commitment of Samoa to the sector.

records.text: 26. While the Constitution of Samoa guarantees freedom of expression, the domestic legal framework does not explicitly establish the right to access information. Public awareness and access to information, especially on the toxic properties of chemicals and products and on the environmental impacts of development projects, is crucial for informed decision-making and to enable meaningful public participation in environmental matters. For example, there is no information on the types of chemicals released from the onsite incinerators at the landfill sites or their impacts on health, impeding the ability of workers on the landfill and neighbouring communities to make informed decisions about their risks of exposure. In addition, the leachate from the Tafaigata landfill contains harmful chemicals such as heavy metals (e.g. lead and mercury), volatile organic compounds and persistent organic pollutants, which contaminate groundwater and pose serious health risks to nearby communities. Illegal burning of waste, including plastic waste, remains common. In his interactions with communities, the Special Rapporteur noted that they were cognizant of plastics as a littering and waste issue, but nothing was mentioned on the negative impacts from the toxic additives in plastics. 27. Surveys and regular monitoring are often hampered by insufficient financial and technical resources, limiting the availability of information. According to the National Waste Management Strategy, the only national body with the capacity to carry out scientific research was the Scientific Research Organisation of Samoa. In some cases, even when data is collected, it is not disaggregated. Data that is disaggregated, including by gender, allows for more informed decision-making, increased capacity for monitoring compliance and a better understanding of differential risks and impacts. 28. According to a 2021 report of the Office of the Ombudsman in Samoa, the most common media used to obtain information on research, news and government policies among the Samoans surveyed are newspapers (35 per cent), social media (31 per cent), the Internet (19 per cent) and submission of information requests (13 per cent). During his visit, the Special Rapporteur noted that several important pieces of legislation were not found online, such as the Waste Management (Importation of Waste for Electricity Generation) Regulations 2015 and the Waste (Plastic Bag) Management Regulations 2018. 29. There are structures within the Samoan traditional system, such as the women’s committee at the village level, that could be leveraged to ensure that women’s perspectives are reflected in consultations on new environmental regulations or in policy development. Their inclusion in those processes could be coordinated in partnership with the Ministry of Women, Community and Social Development.

records.text: 20. The Government’s annual funding of the environmental sector has been consistent over the past decade, averaging 20–27 million Samoan tala annually. Those funds cover the salaries of key personnel, operational costs and some capital costs. However, that amount is insufficient to meet the various challenges, and the lack of adequate financial and human resources greatly impedes monitoring and enforcement of environmental laws. The National Waste Management Strategy indicates that, while the Ministry of Natural Resources and Environment stands ready to fulfil its responsibilities under the Waste Management Act, its insufficient capacity limits its ability to fulfil its obligations. Development partners have supported the environmental sector in Samoa, contributing close to $100 million, constituting the main source of external funding over the past decade. 21. In some circumstances, there is overlap or confusion about the roles and responsibilities of various authorities, which contributes to the enforcement challenge. For example, the Waste Management Act lists the management of landfills as one of the functions of the Ministry of Natural Resources and Environment. Yet in 2019, that function was transferred to the Ministry of Works, Transport and Infrastructure to streamline waste management operations. There seems to be a need to review the current legislation to clarify the function and accountability of each entity, particularly with respect to planning and development. 22. A large degree of environmental governance also lies with villages and village authorities. The fa’amatai, which could be described as the native political system, is central to the organization of Samoan society. Most Samoans reside in villages consisting of groups of families with close ties. The matai, holders of family chief titles, oversee the welfare and well-being of their aiga, or family. Each aiga designates at least one matai to represent it at the village council, the fono, which deals with most civil and criminal matters at the village level and serves as the executive and judicial authority of every village. It is important to note that members of the national legislative assembly must be matai title holders in their villages. According to the 2020 voluntary national review of Samoa on the implementation of the Sustainable Development Goals, only 22 per cent of registered matai are women. 23. One of the key functions of the fa’amatai system is protection of the aiga’s property, particularly customary land. About 81 per cent of land in Samoa is customary, 15 per cent is government-owned and 4 per cent is freehold. Customary land is protected under the Constitution and cannot be sold, traded or used as collateral. Accordingly, coordination between the central Government and matai and village authorities is key to environmental governance. For instance, the matai from Sili turned down a government proposal to construct a hydroelectric plant in the village for environmental reasons. Other positive examples include the villages of Uafato on Upolu and Falealupo on Savai’, which have committed to conservation efforts. 24. Village by-laws and village council decisions can also be used to promote sustainable practices and environmental protection at the village level. The Village Fono Act 1990 recognizes village by-laws, which give traditional village fonos the authority to manage village affairs, either independently or in coordination with government ministries. The effectiveness of village by-laws stems from their alignment with Samoan cultural values and local ownership. While there is no legal provision for enforcement, loyalty and the weight of community opinion act as the main incentive for compliance. According to the Samoa state of the environment report 2023, 45 villages have by-laws that oversee the environment, including by regulating land use, addressing waste management practices and promoting conservation efforts. The matai and village authorities play an integral role in ensuring compliance through various practices, including traditional mechanisms. 25. Most villages have a women’s committee, or komiti. It has been stated that women’s committees are in charge of public health and overseeing community cleanliness. Yet, regulating waste management at the village level seems to be the role of the fono, which is mostly dominated by men. The day-to-day activities of waste management, household cleaning and gardening seem to fall to women in the village. As in many societies globally, this increases women’s exposure to chemicals and toxic fumes. While the formal waste management sector continues to be dominated by men, two of the key recycling organizations in Samoa – the Samoa Recycling and Waste Management Association and the Samoa and Tokelau Association of Recyclers – are led by women.

records.section: Domestic legal framework and environmental governance
records.text: 18. The Constitution of Samoa came into force when the country gained independence from New Zealand in 1962. Part II of the Constitution provides for several fundamental rights and empowers the Supreme Court to take the necessary action to secure those rights. Despite several amendments to the Constitution and the adoption of new laws, the right to a clean, healthy and sustainable environment has yet to be integrated in the Samoan legal framework. 19. Samoa has a relatively well-developed legislative framework for waste management compared to many other Pacific small island developing States, thanks to the Waste Management Act 2010. The Act designates the Ministry of Natural Resources and Environment as the chief authority responsible for waste management, outlining 17 functions it must carry out. It covers the collection, management, disposal and recycling of waste. It also provides for the licensing of waste operators, dumping and incineration permits, outlining environmental standards and structuring community involvement. It is complemented by other planning and environmental laws, including the Agriculture and Fisheries Ordinance 1959, the Lands, Surveys and Environment Act 1989, the Planning and Urban Management Act 2004 and the Water Resources Management Act 2008, among others. Moreover, supporting regulations have been developed under the Waste Management Act such as the Waste (Plastic Bag) Management Regulations 2018, which ban the import, manufacture, export, sale and distribution of plastic bags, plastic packing bags and plastic straws. While administration of the Waste Management Act is centralized in the Ministry of Natural Resources and Environment, other agencies play important roles in administering waste management activities. For example, the Planning and Urban Management Act is now the responsibility of the Ministry of Works, Transport and Infrastructure.

records.text: 12. Samoa was the first small island State in the Pacific to gain independence, in 1962. Almost 15 years later, it joined the United Nations as the one hundred and forty-seventh Member. Since then, Samoa has ratified six out of the nine core human rights treaties and has had a standing invitation to the special procedures in place since 2011. Samoa has yet to ratify the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights and the International Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Racial Discrimination, among others. In view of the indivisibility and interdependence of all human rights, the lack of recognition and justiciability of economic, social and cultural rights, in particular, can negatively impact the right to a clean, healthy and sustainable environment. 13. Samoa has ratified the key multilateral environmental agreements on chemicals and wastes (the Basel Convention on the Control of Transboundary Movements of Hazardous Wastes and Their Disposal, the Rotterdam Convention on the Prior Informed Consent Procedure for Certain Hazardous Chemicals and Pesticides in International Trade, the Stockholm Convention on Persistent Organic Pollutants, the Minamata Convention on Mercury and the Montreal Protocol on Substances that Deplete the Ozone Layer). In the region, Samoa is also party to the Convention to Ban the Importation into Forum Island Countries of Hazardous and Radioactive Wastes and to Control the Transboundary Movement of Hazardous Wastes within the South Pacific Region (Waigani Convention). Samoa was in fact among the first States to ratify the Minamata Convention on Mercury, viewing it as a crucial step for small island developing States vulnerable to mercury pollution. 14. The compliance rate of Samoa with notification, information-sharing and reporting obligations under these agreements is among the highest of the Pacific small island States. This is largely due to its Waste Management Act 2010, specifically section 15 thereof, which designates the Ministry of Natural Resources and Environment as the lead entity responsible for compliance with and implementation of these agreements. The Act lists all the relevant environmental agreements to which Samoa is a party, but it has yet to be amended to include the Minamata Convention on Mercury. Despite the relatively high compliance rate, Samoa faces significant challenges meeting the reporting requirements, as capacity and resources are overstretched, with one official sometimes covering reporting for several agreements. 15. Samoa has taken on a leadership role in driving environmental stewardship at the regional and international levels. It hosts the Secretariat of the Pacific Regional Environment Programme, a regional organization and crucial actor for environmental protection and sustainable development in the Pacific, providing technical support, capacity-building and coordination for its 26 member States. In 2023–2024, Samoa chaired the Alliance of Small Island States (AOSIS), which plays a key role in advancing the priorities of small island developing States in international climate and development negotiations. 16. Samoa has taken strong stances on several global environmental issues. At the second United Nations Conference to Support the Implementation of Sustainable Development Goal 14: Conserve and sustainably use the oceans, seas and marine resources for sustainable development (United Nations Ocean Conference), held in Lisbon in 2022, Samoa joined an alliance calling for a moratorium on deep-sea mining. Moreover, in the negotiations on an international legally binding treaty on plastic pollution, including in the marine environment, Samoa called for an ambitious, effective and equitable treaty that takes a full life-cycle approach. It underscored the specific circumstances that small island developing States face, whether in terms of participation in the negotiations or implementation, asserting that an effective instrument for those States must include a robust financing mechanism, technology transfer and capacity-building. In 2024, Vanuatu, together with Fiji and Samoa, submitted a proposal to the International Criminal Court to amend the Rome Statute to recognize ecocide as an international crime. 17. Regionally, the 2050 Strategy for the Blue Pacific Continent sets out a common approach for securing the future of the Pacific. The Strategy is centred around the connection to the natural environment, cultural values and traditional knowledge. Cleaner Pacific 2025: Pacific Regional Waste and Pollution Management Strategy 2016–2025 is another regional long-term strategy, specifically focused on integrated and sustainable waste management and pollution prevention. Many of the national programmes of Samoa are guided by those regional initiatives.

records.text: 6. Samoa is a small island developing State in the central South Pacific, consisting of four inhabited islands and several small uninhabited islands. The two main islands are Upolu and Savai’i. Upolu is the most populous island, where about 77 per cent of the population resides. Savai’i is the largest island in terms of surface area and is home to about 22 per cent of the population. 7. The ocean constitutes about 98 per cent of the domain of Samoa. These waters support biodiverse coral reefs and a wide range of marine animals, including globally important and threatened species, such as whales, sea turtles and dugongs, among others. 8. In addition to their cultural value, land and marine systems have been the mainstay for the Samoan people, providing them with food, transport, economic opportunity, shelter and fuel. While agriculture, fishing and tourism are key sectors in the national economy, for rural communities, which represent 82 per cent of the total population of Samoa, the subsistence economy remains the primary source of income and local food production. According to the 2023 Samoa state of the environment report, 94 per cent of households are engaged in agricultural production for sustenance or commercial production, and lagoon systems are favoured fishing areas for about 86 per cent of Samoan households. 9. The natural resources of Samoa are increasingly under threat due to a range of pressures and specific economic challenges, despite their central role in Fa’a Samoa (the Samoan way of life). Between 2016 and 2021, the population of Samoa increased by 4.9 per cent, with the most recent census noting a continuous migration to Upolu in search of better educational and employment opportunities. The lifestyles of Samoans are also changing, with an increasing reliance on imported goods that include plastic packaging and waste materials. 10. Samoa is often on the receiving end of action taken thousands of miles away. Despite its minimal contribution to global greenhouse gas emissions, Samoa is among the countries most affected by the adverse impacts of climate change, like many other small island developing States. The economic losses of Samoa have averaged 46 per cent of their gross domestic product (GDP) during disaster years. Moreover, 70 per cent of the population and the infrastructure of Samoa is in low-lying coastal areas and sea level rise risks causing coastal erosion, damage to property and displacement. Furthermore, extreme weather events could damage or overwhelm waste management infrastructure, release toxic chemicals and leachate, and pollute land and groundwater. 11. Adding to these environmental pressures, small island developing States, including Samoa, confront specific economic and trade constraints. The country’s remoteness makes access to international markets difficult and transportation costs high. In addition, there is limited land availability and the small size of the country makes it difficult to achieve economies of scale. These factors limit the economic options and solutions available to small island developing States, contributing to Samoa ranking thirteenth among the 127 countries most reliant on foreign aid.

records.text: 43. The Committee commends the State party on the establishment of a Family Court, in 2014, which is presided over by a female Supreme Court judge. In the light of its general comment No. 13 (2011) on the right of the child to freedom from all forms of violence and taking note of target 16.2 of the Sustainable Development Goals on ending abuse, exploitation, trafficking and all forms of violence against and torture of children, the Committee recommends that the State party: (a) Encourage community-based programmes aimed at preventing and tackling domestic violence, child abuse and neglect, sexual exploitation and abuse, and pay particular attention to and address the gender dimension of violence; (b) Take all measures necessary to ensure that child victims of violence receive psychological and recovery services, that they are aware of the reporting procedure and the existence of protection orders, and that they are encouraged to report cases of domestic violence, in particular child sexual abuse, to the authorities; (c) Amend legislation to ensure that all sexual acts involving children are criminalized as a separate crime, that the definition of rape is gender-neutral and that the protection of persons who report incidents of violence against children is included in the Family Safety Act of 2013; (d) Conduct awareness-raising activities to combat the stigmatization of children born out of wedlock, which can lead to their abandonment, and the stigmatization of child victims of sexual exploitation and abuse, including incest, and ensure accessible, confidential, child-friendly and effective reporting channels for such violations; (e) Provide a legal framework and mechanisms for monitoring the non-governmental organizations offering services and assistance to child victims by adopting the Child Care and Protection Bill; (f) Take all measures necessary to ensure that the Domestic Violence Unit of the police has adequate human, technical and financial resources, particularly for specialized personnel dealing with cases of violence against children, to enable it to offer counselling services, and that sufficient support is provided to non-governmental organizations that provide shelter, counselling and rehabilitation services to child victims of abuse; (g) Systematically collect information on all cases of domestic violence against children, including sexual abuse, child abuse, incest, neglect, ill-treatment and domestic violence, and undertake a comprehensive assessment of the extent, causes and nature of such violence.

records.text: 20. The Committee recognizes the rich culture and traditions of the State party and their importance in daily life. The Committee expresses its serious concern, however, about the persistence of harmful norms, practices, traditions, patriarchal attitudes and deep-rooted stereotypes regarding the roles, responsibilities and identities of women and men in all spheres of life, in addition to the State party’s limited efforts to tackle such discriminatory practices. These include, in particular, women’s limited access to family chiefly titles (matai), discrimination against women married to untitled men and the practice of banishing families from the village by village councils. records.section: Visibility of the Convention and the Committee’s general recommendations
records.text: 10. The Committee is concerned at the general lack of awareness of the Convention, its concept of substantive gender equality and of the Committee’s general recommendations in the State party, in particular among the judiciary and other law enforcement officials. It is further concerned that women themselves, especially those in rural and remote areas, are unaware of their rights under the Convention and thus lack the information necessary to claim their rights.

records.text: 9. While reaffirming that the Government has the primary responsibility and is particularly accountable for the full implementation of the obligations of the State party under the Convention, the Committee stresses that the Convention is binding on all branches of the Government and invites the State party to encourage Parliament, in line with its procedures, where appropriate, to take the steps necessary to implement the present concluding observations between now and the Government’s subsequent reporting process under the Convention.
themes: Cooperation & Follow up with Treaty Bodies

records.section: C. Principal areas of concern and recommendations
records.text: 8. The Committee recalls the obligation of the State party to systematically and continuously implement all the provisions of the Convention and views the concerns and recommendations identified in the present concluding observations as requiring the priority attention of the State party between now and the submission of the subsequent periodic report. Consequently, the Committee urges the State party to focus on those areas in its implementation activities and to report on actions taken and results achieved in its subsequent periodic report. The Committee calls upon the State party to submit the present concluding observations to all relevant ministries, to Parliament and to the judiciary so as to ensure their full implementation.
